questions.title: S3 Integration with Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: Use the AWS SDK v2 S3Client (or Spring Cloud AWS's S3Template) to upload objects with PutObjectRequest, download with GetObjectRequest, and generate presigned URLs with S3Presigner. Always use IAM roles for authentication — never hardcode access keys.

sections.title: The Architecture Mistake: Routing File Bytes Through Your Application Server
sections.content:
The naive approach to file uploads is: client sends a multipart POST to your Spring Boot controller, the controller reads the file into memory, then uploads it to S3. For a 10 MB profile picture, this works. For a 500 MB video or 10,000 concurrent uploads, your application server becomes a **file proxy** — consuming heap memory, network bandwidth, and Tomcat threads for data that's just passing through.

The production pattern is **presigned URLs**: your Spring Boot server generates a time-limited URL that authorizes the client to upload or download directly to/from S3. The server handles only the URL generation (milliseconds), and the client handles the data transfer (seconds to minutes). Your application never touches the file bytes.

This distinction — proxying bytes vs. generating presigned URLs — is what interviewers are testing. Both approaches use the same S3 SDK, but the presigned URL pattern demonstrates an understanding of how production systems handle file operations at scale.

sections.title: Streaming Uploads and Downloads: When Your Server Must Handle Bytes
Presigned URLs: The Pattern That Scales File Operations Without Server Cost
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Presigned URL for uploads/downloads skips the server** — client uploads directly to S3; server generates a time-limited signed URL; eliminates server bandwidth, memory, and connection usage for file transfer
- **`S3Client.putObject` with streaming avoids loading files into memory** — use `RequestBody.fromInputStream()` with a content length; never buffer large files in a byte array before uploading
- **`S3Template` from Spring Cloud AWS simplifies common operations** — wraps SDK client with Spring idioms; inherits IAM credential resolution from the task or instance role automatically
- **Never make buckets public; use presigned or CloudFront signed URLs** — presigned URLs expire after a configured duration (15 min to 7 days); CloudFront signed URLs allow longer expiry with CDN distribution
- **Enable versioning and SSE on user-upload buckets** — versioning recovers accidental overwrites; SSE-S3 (or SSE-KMS for key management compliance) encrypts all objects at rest

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
S3 integration in Spring Boot comes down to one architectural decision: does your server proxy the file bytes through itself, or does it generate a presigned URL and let the client upload or download directly?

**Presigned URLs — the right default**
- A presigned URL is a time-limited S3 URL that grants the holder permission to read or write a specific object — your server generates it with `S3Presigner.presignPutObject()` and returns it to the client, which then uploads directly to S3
- This is the correct approach for uploads because the file never passes through your server — which means your server doesn't consume bandwidth, memory, or connection slots for large uploads; S3 handles the inbound data transfer directly

**Direct upload via the server — when necessary**
- If you need to validate, transform, or virus-scan the file before storing it, the server must receive the bytes — use `S3Client.putObject(PutObjectRequest, RequestBody.fromInputStream(stream, length))` with a streaming approach to avoid loading the entire file into memory
- Set `Content-Type` and `ContentDisposition` on the PutObjectRequest so S3 serves the file with the correct headers when downloaded

**Using Spring Cloud AWS**
- `spring-cloud-aws-starter-s3` provides `S3Template` which wraps the SDK client with Spring idioms — `s3Template.upload(bucket, key, inputStream)` for uploads, `s3Template.download(bucket, key)` returns a `Resource`
- Inject `S3Template` as a bean; Spring Cloud AWS handles credential resolution from the IAM task role automatically in ECS

**Access control**
- Never make buckets public; use presigned URLs for time-limited access; for long-term sharing, generate CloudFront signed URLs through a distribution in front of S3
- Enable S3 bucket versioning for user-uploaded data so accidental overwrites can be recovered; enable server-side encryption (SSE-S3 or SSE-KMS) for compliance

questions.question: How do you optimize S3 costs using storage classes and lifecycle policies?
questions.title: S3 Storage Classes and Lifecycle: Cost Optimization
questions.direct_answer: Match storage class to access pattern: **Standard** for frequently accessed (default); **Standard-IA / One Zone-IA** for infrequent access (30+ day lifetime); **Intelligent-Tiering** when access patterns are unknown — AWS moves objects automatically; **Glacier Instant** for quarterly access; **Glacier Flexible / Deep Archive** for compliance archives. Set lifecycle rules from day one to transition old objects automatically. For a 100TB bucket, correct tiering cuts cost from ~$2,300/mo to ~$400/mo (IA) or ~$40/mo (Glacier).

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical FinOps knowledge; understanding S3 cost drivers beyond just storage-per-GB
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Leaving all objects on Standard forever, or picking One Zone-IA for critical data (no AZ redundancy)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss Intelligent-Tiering for variable workloads, retrieval costs of Glacier, S3 Storage Lens for analysis, and request costs (PUT/GET) as separate cost driver

sections.title: S3 Has Seven Storage Classes — Pick by Access Pattern
sections.content:
S3 storage cost is one of the most commonly wasted spends on AWS. The default S3 Standard is great for frequently accessed data but costs 5–60x more per GB than archival classes. A 100TB bucket on Standard: ~$2,300/month. The same bucket on IA: ~$400/month. On Glacier Deep Archive: ~$40/month.

The seven classes, ordered by cost:

1. **S3 Standard** ($0.023/GB) — default; multi-AZ; best for frequently accessed data like app assets, hot analytics
2. **S3 Intelligent-Tiering** ($0.023/GB + monitoring fee) — AWS automatically moves objects between tiers based on access patterns; no retrieval fees; use when you don't know access patterns
3. **S3 Standard-IA** ($0.0125/GB) — infrequent access but needs immediate availability; multi-AZ; 30-day minimum; retrieval costs apply
4. **S3 One Zone-IA** ($0.01/GB) — same as IA but single AZ; 20% cheaper but less durable; for recreatable data
5. **S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval** ($0.004/GB) — archive with millisecond retrieval; for quarterly-access compliance data
6. **S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval** ($0.0036/GB) — minutes to hours retrieval; cheaper still
7. **S3 Glacier Deep Archive** ($0.00099/GB) — 12-hour retrieval; the cheapest; long-term compliance

**Lifecycle rules** are the mechanism: "transition objects to IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90 days, expire after 7 years." Set these up once, AWS handles the rest.

sections.title: Setting Up Lifecycle Rules
Trade-offs and Hidden Cost Drivers
sections.content:
**Retrieval costs matter.** IA charges $0.01/GB retrieval; Glacier Flexible charges $0.01–0.10/GB depending on speed; Deep Archive charges on retrieval. If you'll access data regularly, IA's retrieval cost can exceed the storage savings. Intelligent-Tiering avoids this with no retrieval fees but charges a monitoring fee ($0.0025 per 1000 objects).

**Minimum storage duration.** IA classes have a 30-day minimum; deleting within 30 days still charges for 30 days. Glacier classes have 90 or 180 day minimums. Don't transition short-lived data.

**Minimum object size.** IA, Glacier Instant have a 128KB minimum billable size. Tiny objects cost more per byte because you pay for 128KB each. For many small objects, Standard or Intelligent-Tiering may be cheaper.

**Request costs are separate from storage.** PUT/COPY/POST: $0.005 per 1000; GET: $0.0004 per 1000. A write-heavy workload on Standard with millions of small objects can cost more in requests than in storage.

**One Zone-IA is only single-AZ.** 20% cheaper than Standard-IA but loses data if the AZ fails. Use only for data you can regenerate (cached results, secondary copies).

**Intelligent-Tiering is great when you don't know.** New bucket with mixed workload? Start with Intelligent-Tiering; let AWS figure out access patterns. You pay a small monitoring fee (~$0.0025/1000 objects/month) but avoid retrieval charges and tier decisions.

**S3 Storage Lens is free and essential.** AWS's built-in analytics shows bucket-level cost breakdown, object age distribution, IA-eligibility. Enable default dashboard (free) to understand your patterns before designing lifecycle.

**Versioning + lifecycle.** If versioning is enabled, old versions accumulate. Use `NoncurrentVersionTransitions` and `NoncurrentVersionExpiration` to manage them separately from current versions.

**Incomplete multipart uploads.** Failed multipart uploads leave parts invisible but billable. Always add `AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload` (7 days) to lifecycle.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Seven storage classes span $0.023/GB (Standard) to $0.00099/GB (Deep Archive)** — 23x cost difference for the same data
- **Lifecycle rules automate transitions** — set once, AWS handles transitions based on object age
- **Intelligent-Tiering for unknown patterns** — AWS moves objects automatically; no retrieval fees; small monitoring cost
- **Retrieval costs matter for IA/Glacier** — frequent access can wipe out storage savings; calculate total cost
- **Minimum billable sizes and durations** — 128KB for IA/Glacier Instant; 30-day minimum for IA; don't transition tiny short-lived data
- **Always abort incomplete multipart uploads** — invisible parts accumulate and bill; add to lifecycle rule
- **S3 Storage Lens (free)** reveals patterns — object age distribution, IA-eligibility, cost breakdown

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
S3 storage cost is one of the most commonly wasted spends on AWS. The default S3 Standard is great for hot data but costs 5 to 60 times more per GB than archival classes. A 100TB bucket on Standard costs $2,300 per month; on Glacier Deep Archive it's $40 per month.

**The seven storage classes, ordered by cost**
- S3 Standard at $0.023/GB — default, multi-AZ, for frequently accessed data
- S3 Intelligent-Tiering at $0.023/GB plus monitoring — AWS moves objects between tiers automatically; use when access patterns are unknown; no retrieval fees
- S3 Standard-IA at $0.0125/GB — infrequent access, immediate availability, multi-AZ, 30-day minimum
- S3 One Zone-IA at $0.01/GB — same as IA but single AZ, 20% cheaper, only for recreatable data
- S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval at $0.004/GB — archive with millisecond retrieval; quarterly access patterns
- S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval at $0.0036/GB — minutes to hours retrieval
- S3 Glacier Deep Archive at $0.00099/GB — 12-hour retrieval; long-term compliance

**Lifecycle rules are the mechanism**
- Set rules like "transition to IA after 30 days, Glacier after 90, expire after 7 years"
- Configured once via bucket policy; AWS handles transitions automatically
- Critical: always add AbortIncompleteMultipartUpload (7 days) — failed multipart uploads leave invisible parts that accumulate and bill

**The hidden cost drivers most teams miss**
- Retrieval costs matter — IA charges $0.01/GB retrieval; if you access data frequently, retrieval cost can exceed storage savings
- Minimum storage duration — IA has 30-day minimum; Glacier has 90-180 day minimum; deleting early still charges for the minimum
- Minimum object size — 128KB for IA and Glacier Instant; tiny objects cost more per byte
- Request costs are separate — PUT at $0.005/1000, GET at $0.0004/1000; write-heavy workloads with millions of small objects may cost more in requests than storage

**The decision rules**
- Frequently accessed (daily): Standard
- Unknown access patterns, mixed: Intelligent-Tiering
- Known infrequent access, need immediate: Standard-IA
- Recreatable data okay with single AZ: One Zone-IA
- Quarterly access compliance data: Glacier Instant Retrieval
- Long-term compliance, slow retrieval OK: Deep Archive

**The tools**
- S3 Storage Lens is free and essential; shows bucket-level cost breakdown, object age distribution, IA-eligibility
- Enable the default dashboard (free) to understand your patterns before designing lifecycle rules
- S3 Intelligent-Tiering when in doubt — pays for itself vs manual tiering mistakes

**The strategic answer**
- Don't leave everything on Standard; set lifecycle rules from day one
- Use Intelligent-Tiering for variable or unknown workloads
- Analyze via Storage Lens monthly; adjust rules as patterns change
- Versioning plus lifecycle needs noncurrent-version rules too, or old versions pile up
